newsitem.title: UK: Clinton to maintain N.Irish interest - Mitchell.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to maintain N.Irish interest - Mitchell.

text.p: The U.S. head of Northern Ireland peace talks, former Senator George Mitchell, said on Wednesday that President Bill Clinton would keep up a "deep and personal" interests in the fortunes of the troubled province in his second term of office.
Playing down speculation that he himself might be named U.S Secretary of State, Mitchell said he remained committed to his job at the helm of the British province's multi-party talks.
"The President's interest in Northern Ireland is deep and personal and will undoubtedly continue," Mitchell told Reuters.
"His roots are here. He has a keen interest in it. It is something that he feels strongly about..."
Clinton, who has Irish ancestors, made a triumphant trip to the partitioned island a year ago to bolster a Northern Irish peace since shattered by guerrilla war.
The visit sealed an Anglo-Irish drive to kickstart a peace process that had been bogged down for months.
But early optimism foundered when the Irish Republican Army ditched a 17-month truce and returned to war last February.
Mitchell, a skilled mediator, was invited by Britain and Ireland to chair multi-party talks that exclude Sinn Fein while the IRA is on the warpath.
"To the extent that he (Clinton) can be helpful, he will be so but he recognises that the decisions here have to be made by all the participants themselves," Mitchell said.
On speculation that he might be made Secretary of State, he said no such offer had been either broached or discussed.

The current incumbent, Warren Christopher, was a good friend, he said. "I think he has done a good job for which he has not got sufficient credit. I think the best thing for President Clinton and for the U.S. would be if Warren Christopher remains as Secretary of State."

Mitchell conceded that if an offer came, he would consider it. But he also made it clear his commitment to the Belfast talks that have made slow progress since their launch in June. "I am here and I intend to stay and to be helpful."
Britain and Ireland invited Mitchell to chair the talks in an effort to establish peace after years of war by rival guerrillas about the future of British rule.

Prime Minister John Bruton told the Dublin parliament that Clinton had been a "great, good and consistent friend to Ireland. We as a country have much to be grateful for in respect of President Clinton's first term."
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams said he looked forward to Clinton's "continued involvement in our efforts to achieve a negotiated peace settlement."
The powerful Protestant Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), which is backed by most of the province's majority Protestants, said its leaders hope to meet Clinton in Washington early next month.
